title: How to Calculate Labor Cost: A Complete Guide
summary: Labor cost is more than wages. Learn how to calculate total labor cost, labor cost percentage, and what it means for your small business's bottom line.
body_markdown:
Just because you hire someone at $15 an hour doesn't mean that's everything you'll need to pay.


By the time you factor in employer payroll taxes, workers' compensation, and benefits like paid time off and health insurance, that $15 hire often costs $18 to $21 an hour. For a small business running on thin margins, that gap is the difference between a profitable week and a rough one.


Most owners figure this out at their first payroll run, when the real bill arrives. This guide closes that gap before it surprises you. We walk through what labor cost actually includes, the formulas for calculating it, how to benchmark it against your industry, and how to use a free tool that does the math for you.

## **How to Calculate Labor Cost: The Short Version**


If you need a quick answer before we get into the details, here it is:


- **Labor cost = wages + employer payroll taxes + benefits + other employment costs**
- The real cost of an employee typically runs 20 to 30% higher than their base wage
- **Labor cost percentage = total labor cost / revenue x 100**
- Industry benchmarks: restaurants typically run 30 to 37%, retail 15 to 30%, service businesses 30 to 50% or more
- You can calculate all of this in minutes with the[free Homebase labor cost calculator](https://www.joinhomebase.com/labor-cost-calculator)


## **What Is Labor Cost?**


[Labor cost](https://www.joinhomebase.com/labor-cost) is the total amount a business spends to employ its team, not just wages. It includes gross pay, employer payroll taxes, benefits like health insurance and paid time off, and other employment-related expenses. For most small businesses, the real cost of an employee runs 20 to 30% higher than their base hourly rate or salary.


This distinction matters for two reasons. First, owners who calculate labor cost as wages only will consistently underestimate what their team costs. Second, labor cost shows up in two forms: as a raw dollar figure (what you spend) and as a percentage of revenue (how efficiently you spend it). Both numbers are useful, and this guide covers both.


### **Wages vs. labor cost at a glance.**


Side-by-side comparison of employee take-home rate vs. total employer labor cost per hour for an $18/hr worker What your team member sees What you actually pay


$18/hr on the timesheet $18/hr in wages


+ $1.38/hr in employer FICA taxes


+ ~$0.90/hr in workers' compensation


+ ~$1.80/hr in paid time off accrual


+ health insurance contribution


**= $22 to $24/hr total**


The items on the right are what accountants call "[labor burden](http://docs.google.com/blog/labor-burden-rate) ." They do not show up on a timecard, but they show up on your books every pay period.


## **What Does Labor Cost Include?**


Labor cost includes four main categories: wages and salaries, employer payroll taxes, employee benefits, and other employment costs.


Wages are the largest piece, averaging about 70% of total compensation for private-sector workers, according to the[Bureau of Labor Statistics](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ecec.htm) . The remaining 30% covers taxes and benefits, and that share varies depending on your state, your benefits package, and your team size.


Here is what goes into each category.


**Wages and salaries**


- Base hourly pay for every hour worked
- [Overtime pay](http://docs.google.com/blog/how-to-calculate-overtime-pay) (time and a half for hours over 40 in a workweek, under federal law)
- Bonuses and commissions
- Shift differentials, if applicable


**Employer payroll taxes**


- [FICA](http://docs.google.com/blog/fica-tax-small-business) **:** You pay 6.2% for Social Security and 1.45% for Medicare on every team member's wages, totaling 7.65%. This is on top of what your team pays from their own checks. The 2026 Social Security wage base is $184,500, per[IRS Publication 926](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p926) .
- [FUTA](http://docs.google.com/blog/what-is-futa-tax) **:** The Federal Unemployment Tax Act charges 6% on the first $7,000 of each employee's wages per year. Most employers receive a 5.4% state credit, bringing the effective rate down to 0.6%, per the[IRS FUTA Credit Reduction](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/futa-credit-reduction) guidelines.
- **SUTA:** State unemployment taxes vary by state and employer history. Check your state's labor department for your current rate.


For a full breakdown of what you owe as an employer, see our guide to[payroll taxes for small business](http://docs.google.com/blog/payroll-taxes-for-small-business) .


**Benefits**


- Employer health, dental, and vision[insurance contributions](http://docs.google.com/blog/employee-benefits-small-business)
- [Paid time off](http://docs.google.com/blog/paid-time-off-pto) , including the cost of hours you pay but are not worked
- [Workers' compensation](http://docs.google.com/blog/workers-compensation-insurance) insurance premiums


**Other employment costs**


- Onboarding and training
- Uniforms or tools you provide
- Background checks
- Employer retirement contributions, if offered


This full picture is what people mean when they say "[fully loaded labor cost](http://docs.google.com/blog/fully-loaded-labor-cost) ." All of it, wages plus everything stacked on top, is what it actually costs to have someone on your team. Getting this breakdown right is the foundation of sound[small business payroll](http://docs.google.com/blog/small-business-payroll-guide) management.


According to the[2026 Bureau of Labor Statistics Employer Costs for Employee Compensation report](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ecec.htm) , private industry workers cost employers an average of $46.60 per hour worked. Wages made up $32.60 of that. Benefits accounted for the remaining $14.01, or 30.1%.


## **The Labor Cost Formula**


The basic labor cost formula is: **Total Labor Cost = Wages + Employer Payroll Taxes + Benefits + Other Employment Costs.**


To find your labor cost percentage, divide total labor cost by total revenue and multiply by 100. For direct labor only, multiply hours worked by hourly wage rate, then add the proportional share of taxes and benefits for those specific workers.


Here are the three formulas you need.


### **Total labor cost formula.**


> **Total Labor Cost = Gross Wages + Employer Payroll Taxes + Benefits + Other Employment Costs**


**Worked example:** A team member earning $18/hr works 40 hours in a week.


- Gross wages: $720
- Employer FICA (7.65%): $55.08
- Workers' comp estimate: $14
- Health insurance contribution: $50
- **Total weekly labor cost: ~$839**
- **Effective hourly rate: ~$21/hr**


### **Direct labor cost formula.**


> **Direct Labor Cost = Hours Worked x Hourly Wage Rate**


[Direct labor](http://docs.google.com/blog/direct-labor-cost) covers team members who directly produce your product or deliver your service: cooks and kitchen workers, sales associates, service technicians. This figure is most useful for pricing, since it tells you the actual labor cost built into each unit of output or hour of service.


### **Labor cost per unit formula.**


> **Labor Cost Per Unit = Total Labor Cost / Units Produced**


This formula applies to businesses that produce a physical product, like a bakery or a custom goods shop. If you spend $2,000 on labor in a week and produce 400 units, your labor cost per unit is $5. Service businesses typically skip this one.


## **How to Calculate Labor Cost Step by Step**


To calculate your total labor cost, start by adding up all gross wages for the period. Then add employer payroll taxes: 7.65% of gross wages for FICA, plus FUTA and SUTA. Next, add benefits, including health insurance contributions, paid time off, and workers' compensation premiums. Finally, include any other employment costs. The total gives you the true cost of your team for that period.


Follow these five steps for any pay period.


1. **List every team member and their gross wages.** Multiply hourly rate by hours worked, then add overtime, bonuses, or commissions for the period.
2. **Calculate employer payroll taxes.** Apply FICA at 7.65% of gross wages. For FUTA, apply 6% to the first $7,000 per employee per year (often 0.6% effective after the state credit). Check your state's SUTA rate separately.
3. **Add benefits costs.** Include your employer contribution to health insurance, the dollar value of paid time off used or accrued, and workers' compensation premiums. If you offer retirement contributions, add those too.
4. **Add any other employment costs.** Think training, uniforms, tools you supply, or onboarding expenses for the period.
5. **Sum everything.** That total is your labor cost for the period.


**Worked example: one week, three team members**


One-week labor cost breakdown for three hourly team members, including wages, FICA taxes, and benefits estimates Team member Hours Rate Gross wages Employer FICA Benefits est. Weekly total


Sarah 35 $18/hr $630 $48.20 $64 $742


Miguel 40 $16/hr $640 $48.96 $64 $753


Devon 25 $15/hr $375 $28.69 $40 $444


Total **100 hrs** — **$1,645** **$125.85** **$168** **$1,939**


In this example, 100 hours of scheduled work costs $1,939, not the $1,645 in wages alone. That $294 gap is the labor burden. Across a full team over a full year, that difference adds up fast.

## **How to Calculate Labor Cost Percentage**


[Labor cost percentage](http://docs.google.com/blog/labor-cost-percentage) shows how much of your revenue goes toward paying your team. Calculate it using this formula: **Labor Cost Percentage = (Total Labor Cost / Total Revenue) x 100** .


If your restaurant brought in $80,000 last month and total labor costs were $24,000, your labor cost percentage is 30%. Benchmarks vary by industry: restaurants typically run 30 to 37%, retail 15 to 30%, and service businesses 30 to 50% or more.


**The formula:**


> **Labor Cost Percentage = (Total Labor Cost / Total Revenue) x 100**


**Why this number matters more than the dollar total**


A restaurant spending $30,000 on labor looks completely different at $80,000 in monthly revenue (37.5%) than at $120,000 (25%). The dollar figure tells you what you spent. The percentage tells you whether your spending is proportional to what the business brought in.


**How often should you run this number?**


Monthly is a baseline, but weekly is better. Labor costs shift with scheduling, overtime, and coverage gaps. If you wait until the end of the month to look, you might be reviewing two weeks of overstaffing you can no longer fix. A weekly check means you can adjust before it affects your margin.


**What moves your labor cost percentage**


- Slow periods with schedules that have not been adjusted for lower traffic
- Unplanned overtime that was not caught before it happened
- High turnover, which creates overlap and extra hours during training
- Seasonal revenue dips when your team size stays the same


Tracking your total labor cost percentage is useful, but tracking it by role gives you the real picture.


Luanne Ronquillo, owner and founder of Ruru Baked, a food and beverage business, discovered she had been scheduling more people for the front of house than the traffic required, and it had been quietly inflating her labor cost percentage for an entire year.


She caught it because she could see hours broken down by role: "I was seeing how much is back of house making, how do I factor that into our COGS, and how much are we staffing front of house? We overstaffed front of house last year because we thought we needed more staff and then it was a little bit slower." Knowing where the hours were going was how she knew where to adjust.


## **How to Calculate Labor Cost Per Hour**


To calculate labor cost per hour, divide your total labor cost, including taxes and benefits, by the total number of hours worked in the same period. For example, if you paid $5,000 in total labor costs for 200 hours of work, your labor cost per hour is $25, not the $18 hourly wage on the timecard. That $7 difference is the labor burden.


**The formula:**


> **Labor Cost Per Hour = Total Labor Cost / Total Hours Worked**


This figure is especially useful for service businesses that price by the hour. If you quote a job at $40/hr and your fully loaded labor cost is $28/hr, your actual margin on labor is about 30%. If your fully loaded cost climbs to $35/hr because of untracked overtime, your margin shrinks to 12.5%.


Overtime hours also inflate this number. A team member who works 45 hours instead of 40 earns[time and a half](http://docs.google.com/blog/overtime-laws-by-state) on those five extra hours, which pushes your per-hour cost up for the entire week.[Tracking hours accurately](http://docs.google.com/blog/how-to-track-employee-hours) is what keeps this number honest, and[time and attendance](http://docs.google.com/blog/time-and-attendance-tracking) data is what makes that possible.


## **Labor Cost Benchmarks by Industry**


Labor cost benchmarks vary significantly by industry.


Full-service restaurants typically run a median of 34 to 37% of revenue. Retail businesses target 15 to 30% depending on segment. Service businesses, including salons, fitness studios, and healthcare providers, often run 30 to 50% or higher because labor is the core product.


There is no universal target, but comparing your percentage to industry averages tells you whether you are operating lean, on track, or above the norm.

Trade aggregation

Service businesses 30–50%+ Salons, fitness, healthcare, home services


Industry average


*These are industry medians, not goals. Your target depends on your revenue model, location, and team structure.*


**A note on the restaurant numbers**


The[National Restaurant Association's 2025 Operations Data Abstract](https://restaurant.org/research-and-media/research/restaurant-economic-insights/analysis-commentary/elevated-labor-costs-had-a-significant-impact-on-restaurant-profitability-in-2024/) , based on more than 900 restaurant operators across the U.S., found that full-service restaurants reported a median[restaurant labor cost](http://docs.google.com/blog/restaurant-labor-cost) of 36.5% of sales in 2024. Profitable full-service operators kept it closer to 34.2%. For limited-service operators, the median was 31.7%, with profitable operators averaging 30%.


Those numbers are higher than the old "25 to 35%" benchmark that circulates in most industry articles. If your restaurant is running above 37%, that is not necessarily a crisis, but it is worth a closer look at your scheduling and overtime patterns.


**What pushes labor cost up**


- High minimum wages in your market
- A labor-intensive service model
- High turnover and continuous onboarding
- Unplanned overtime from inconsistent scheduling


**What keeps it in range**


- Scheduling against your actual revenue forecast
- Visibility into hours by role and department
- Catching overtime before it happens, not after

## **How to Reduce Labor Cost Without Cutting Your Team**


Reducing labor cost does not mean cutting hours or letting people go. The most effective strategies target the gaps that inflate costs without adding value: unplanned overtime, overstaffing during slow periods, time theft, and payroll errors that go unnoticed until payday. Small scheduling and time tracking adjustments can meaningfully lower your labor cost percentage without affecting service quality or team morale.


Here are six approaches worth acting on:


- ‍ **Watch for overtime before it happens, not after.** Most overtime is not planned. It builds up because a manager does not see who is approaching 40 hours until it is too late to adjust. Tools that alert you when someone is close to their limit let you swap a shift instead of[paying time and a half](http://docs.google.com/blog/how-to-calculate-overtime-pay) for a whole extra day. Homebase's[employee scheduling](http://docs.google.com/blog/employee-scheduling-software) tool surfaces those alerts before the threshold is crossed, so you can make the call while you still have options.
- **Schedule to your revenue forecast, not last week's schedule.** Copying last week's schedule is fast, but it misses the natural peaks and dips that should drive your headcount. A slow Tuesday in January should not be staffed like a busy Saturday in July. Aligning your schedule to your revenue trends keeps labor spending proportional to what the business is actually bringing in. See our guide on[how to make a work schedule](http://docs.google.com/blog/how-to-make-a-work-schedule) for a step-by-step approach.
- **Track time accurately.** Every untracked overtime minute or uncaught early clock-in adds to your actual labor cost above what you planned for. Digital[time tracking](http://docs.google.com/blog/how-to-track-employee-hours) closes the gap between the hours you scheduled and the hours you actually paid. Homebase's time clock tracks hours from phones, tablets, and computers, and flags discrepancies before they become a payroll issue.
- **Check your labor cost percentage weekly, not monthly.** By the time you review monthly numbers, two or three weeks of overspending have already happened. A weekly check means you can course-correct while there is still time. Tracking this number week over week also helps you see seasonal patterns that would be invisible in a monthly view.
- **Cross-train your team.** When one person can cover two roles, you need fewer bodies during coverage emergencies. Cross-training reduces last-minute callouts and the expensive scramble to fill gaps with overtime or a new hire who is not yet up to speed.
- **Review benefits and perks annually.** Some[employee benefits](http://docs.google.com/blog/employee-benefits-small-business) carry high costs but generate little loyalty. An annual conversation with your team about what they actually value helps you put money where it matters most, and cut where it does not.

## **Frequently Asked Questions About Labor Cost**


### **What is the formula for labor cost?**


Total Labor Cost = Wages + Employer Payroll Taxes + Benefits + Other Employment Costs. To get your labor cost percentage, divide total labor cost by revenue and multiply by 100.


### **How much does a $20 an hour employee cost an employer?**


After adding employer FICA taxes (7.65%), workers' comp, health insurance, and paid time off, a $20/hr employee typically costs $24 to $28/hr in total. At 40 hours per week, that is roughly $50,000 to $58,000 annually. \[WRITER: verify against current IRS rates before publishing.\]


### **How do you estimate labor cost?**


Multiply each team member's hourly rate by expected hours to get gross wages, then add 15 to 30% for payroll taxes, benefits, and other employment costs. The exact percentage depends on your benefits package.


### **What does 30% labor mean?**


It means labor expenses equal 30% of revenue. On $100,000 a month, that is $30,000 on wages, taxes, and benefits. Whether that is good depends on your industry: it is lean for restaurants (median: 31 to 37%), high for retail (target: 15 to 30%), and right in range for most service businesses.


### **What is a good labor cost percentage?**


It depends on your industry. Full-service restaurants typically run 34 to 37%, retail 15 to 30%, and service businesses 30 to 50% or more. If you are consistently above your industry's range, check scheduling patterns and overtime before making bigger changes.


### **What is the difference between direct and indirect labor cost?**


[Direct labor](http://docs.google.com/blog/direct-labor-cost) is the cost of team members who produce your product or deliver your service.[Indirect labor](http://docs.google.com/blog/indirect-labor-cost) covers everyone who supports operations but does not directly produce, like managers and administrators. Direct labor goes into cost of goods sold. Indirect labor is overhead.


## **Stop Reacting to Labor Costs. Start Planning Around Them.**


Labor cost is not a mystery. Once you know what goes into it, wages plus payroll taxes plus benefits plus everything else, the number becomes something you can plan around rather than react to.


Most small business owners who feel like their labor costs keep climbing are dealing with a gap between what they think they pay and what they actually pay. The math in this guide closes that gap.
